links.label: Archival images and the production build

cards.answer: I'd design it the way the archival pipeline is built, where hosted AI services are excluded outright. First, map the network precisely, because "no internet" is usually narrower than that; ours blocked Hugging Face only, so model weights come in through a documented staging path and get pinned by digest so a moved tag can't change the model. Serve with vLLM on the customer's GPU for continuous batching, behind a backend router so either vLLM or Ollama can serve by config. Keep embeddings, the vector index, extracted text and originals inside the network. Order the pipeline so cheap deterministic filters run first and the model only sees what survives. Make every long job checkpoint and resume, and route alerts through whatever the host allows; on our server that's local sendmail, since SMTP is locked down. Then get written confirmation from the customer's privacy office that local open-weight processing is acceptable.

cards.title: Design: integrating with a client's Oracle databases
questions: writing model output back to an oracle schema

how would she connect to an enterprise data warehouse
how do you avoid reprocessing the whole oracle table every run
post write verification against oracle
reading blobs out of oracle
cards.answer: Read narrowly, write reversibly, verify inside the run. The research proposals pipeline does change detection with an anti-join between attachment IDs in the source Kuali tables and those already processed, so each run touches only new documents and "nothing new" exits cleanly as a success. It pulls BLOBs in batches of 20, converts them to PDF, tolerates null or unconvertible files as logged warnings, and keeps credentials in a YAML config, never in code. Before every write it prints rollback SQL with the exact IDs and timestamp filter; afterward it counts rows in the destination and raises if the count falls short. The warehouse for the retirement report required Oracle Native Network Encryption, which thin mode can't negotiate, so it runs python-oracledb in thick mode, documented for Windows and Linux. All SQL lives in version-controlled files, and historical reads are effective-dated, never the current row.

cards.answer: I build the inventory from Box metadata before downloading a byte. The archival ingest constructs the manifest from name, size, SHA-1, path and timestamps alone, so inventory, deduplication and structural filtering all run first, and it checkpoints so a reclaimed Colab session resumes instead of restarting. Stage 01 sits behind a source-adapter boundary: it takes a root path and walks it, whether that's a mounted drive, an SMB share, a forensic disk image or a Box folder. Ingest and delivery are separate layers on purpose, because Box is a poor fit for the first and a good fit for the second. The earlier file-search proof of concept used the Box SDK to enumerate and download a whole folder while keeping every Box path, so search results link back to the original file. One finding mattered: our Box accessions were extracts copied from drives, so numbers derived from them stay provisional.

cards.answer: The daily job starts with a LegiScan hash check, one API call regardless of bill count, and downloads only the sessions whose hash changed. Then it parses the JSON bill files, labels the new actions, rescores changed bills, builds an active-bills snapshot and uploads the session parquets to Azure Blob before saving the new hash. The integration bug worth knowing: the deployed prediction tab matched almost nothing. Older CSVs came from bulk exports with 5-digit internal IDs, while the server parsed real 7-digit LegiScan bill IDs from JSON, so only about 8,820 of 50,501 bills joined, and those by numeric collision. I deleted the stored CSVs, rebuilt everything from the JSON source, and added bill_number as a stable secondary join key in every prediction parquet, then verified it on live data.

cards.answer: The university Entra tenant enforces SSO on the deployment (SCM) endpoint, which breaks standard zip-deploy and publish-profile paths. The reliable route turned out to be Azure Cloud Shell with a remote build (az functionapp deployment source config-zip with build-remote), after sorting out cross-subscription defaults and file-share provisioning. Subscription-level resource-provider permissions also blocked the Flex Consumption plan, so I hosted the Function App on the existing App Service plan instead. The web app had its own blockers when I first deployed it: a .deployment file stopping the Oryx build, missing dependency installation, SCM basic auth configuration and dynamic port binding. There was no existing deployment infrastructure, so I configured environment variables, the startup command and the Local Git plus Oryx pipeline from scratch. I operate it with the Azure CLI for deploys, log inspection and live diagnostics.

questions: the campus firewall blocked cosmos db what did you do

cards.answer: Mid-build I found the analytics server could reach Blob Storage but not Cosmos DB: the Cosmos endpoint was terminated at the TLS level at the campus boundary. That meant the on-prem pipeline couldn't read user prompts or write scores. I re-architected the data path around it. A serverless function exports user profiles and impact prompts from Cosmos to Blob; the server scores them against the local Llama model on vLLM; results go back to Blob as a long-format parquet, one row per user, prompt and bill; and the web app reads them through a dedicated loader with per-user filtering and cached reads. I kept a cache-first live path in the app that scores one bill on demand and writes the same schema, so batch and on-demand results are interchangeable. The split became a deliberate property: heavy batch inference on owned GPU hardware, low-latency requests on managed cloud inference.

cards.title: App Service failure modes: crash loops, cold starts, stale workers

cards.answer: Three are worth describing. First, an outage: the startup command reinstalled dependencies on every container boot, the install failed, and the container died with exit code 127. Users saw a page that kept refreshing. I changed it to a launch-only command with dependencies baked into the Oryx build. Second, a reliability cluster: semantic search failing under memory pressure and cache loss on cold start. I traced those to a shared cause, loaded columns and sessions selectively, configured always-on and start-time limits, and wrote a tier analysis that moved the plan from Basic to Premium v3 for the platform's memory-bound startup. Third, after a Functions deploy, output that read like a code regression was really stale workers serving the previous code. The standing remedy is restart, wait for warm-up, then trigger, plus a one-glance test that the new code is genuinely live.

cards.answer: The legislation pipeline had a backend-agnostic service module from day one: a router picks Ollama or vLLM by a config flag, and the pipeline code never changes. I built it before vLLM was even deployable, because the lesson from the earlier summarization pipeline was that serving infrastructure is the lever to design around, not the model. Once vLLM was serving, the extraction model re-evaluation ran on it in May 2026. The image work showed why the serving layer matters: on the same L4, Ollama serialized requests with throughput flat at about 9 images per minute and the GPU 28 to 31% busy, while vLLM scaled to 55.4 images per minute at concurrency 8, a 6.22x speedup on the same hardware.

cards.answer: Sign-in is a magic link built end to end. The app accepts only university email domains, issues an HMAC-signed one-time token, stores it in Cosmos DB with a TTL so it expires on its own, and sends the link through Azure Communication Services from a verified sender domain. A successful sign-in creates a server-side session record with a configurable multi-day TTL. One gate governs every page, and sessions are restored from the URL so a login survives a page refresh or a container recycle, which matters on App Service. Early on there was also a legacy admin password for demos. I removed it entirely, so university magic-link sign-in is the only route in. The same managed email service delivers the digests, so one verified domain covers both.

questions: how did you design the cosmos db schema

cards.answer: Cosmos DB is the platform's user-data store: profiles, magic-link tokens, sessions, saved items (tracked bills, categories, impact prompts) and impact-scoring results, with partition keys designed per container and TTL policies so tokens and sessions expire without cleanup jobs. The live app and the nightly scorer share incremental-write patterns and one result schema. The nightly function rescores only bills whose content hash changed, so a quiet night costs almost nothing. The in-app path is cache-first: a bill and prompt pair is scored once, stored, and read instantly after that. Profiles feed the model directly, so I put explicit limits on profile and prompt length to keep user-written context from silently truncating the prompt, and documented why for users. Once the campus firewall cut the server off from Cosmos, batch results moved to Blob with the same shape.

cards.answer: I pick the stack that gets a working tool to users fastest without creating a deployment I can't support. For data-heavy internal apps that's Python end to end: the legislative platform is a multi-page Streamlit app using st.navigation, with app.py as a thin router, pages in their own folder, a shared accessible theme and one central auth gate. For procurement I built a FastAPI service with 10 endpoints and a vanilla HTML and JavaScript client with no framework, so it runs as a local file or deployed. To prove an interaction first, I prototype in a standalone HTML page, as I did with the bill prediction view over 6,556 bills, fed by a 5 MB JSON because the raw CSVs were too big for a browser. For payroll the interface is a Box folder: staff upload files and a GitHub Actions workflow runs the pipeline in one click.

cards.answer: Anything that acts on its own gets two gates. The weekly digest function runs behind a dry-run flag and a test-recipient redirect, so every digest can be inspected before a real recipient sees one. I verified personalization end to end across multiple users on July 11, 2026: the same bill appeared in different digests framed differently, as a data-governance obligation for one reader and an AI-ethics question for another, which showed it wasn't keyword matching. Review also caught over-reach: a speed-limit bill rated high-impact for an AI-ethics reader because of an incidental AI-camera provision, so I flagged threshold tightening rather than ship a tenuous inference. Then I held the switch until stakeholders were onboarded in person, because an unexplained autonomous AI email is a worse first impression than none. Before launch I validated digest output against stored profiles and built a pre-launch checklist.

links.label: Archival images and the production build

cards.answer: One L4 with 23 GB of VRAM serves several concurrent workloads, so memory and the host itself are the things to watch. From August 24 to September 3, 2026, legislative extraction failed silently for 11 nights; the cause was a server kernel update that disabled the GPU driver. I documented the cause for the system administrators, protected the catch-up so no data would be skipped, and restored the nightly scoring job. In early September I freed roughly 15 GB of shared GPU memory by right-sizing the language model's allocation, so the archival pipeline could run on the same server. Earlier, Ollama's keep_alive policy had been holding about 6 GB and blocking vLLM's cache. When the shared JupyterHub went down from an out-of-memory failure, I restored it and moved heavy jobs off it so it wouldn't recur.

questions: what runs in the cloud and what runs on the server

cards.answer: Heavy work runs on-prem, user-facing work runs in Azure, and Blob Storage is the seam. On the Linux server with the L4: ingestion, chunking, LLM feature extraction, standardization, embeddings and the FAISS index, plus a daily prediction job scheduled through JupyterHub Scheduler at 4 AM that rescores changed bills and uploads session parquets to Blob. In Azure: the Streamlit app on App Service, reading Blob with a one-hour cache TTL so the morning rescore is visible the same day; a Function App on the same plan for weekly digests and nightly impact scoring; Cosmos DB for user data; Communication Services for sign-in links and email; and Azure OpenAI gpt-4o-mini for on-demand briefings. Batch inference on owned hardware has no marginal cost, and managed cloud inference handles low-latency in-app requests. I designed, provisioned and operate all of it.

questions: what changes between a proof of concept and production

cards.answer: Production means the system tells the truth about itself, survives bad inputs, and can be run by someone other than me. Between the approved February 2026 beta and the production version delivered to IGPA on August 11, 2026, I replaced a shared admin password with magic-link sign-in, made extraction idempotent so a multi-night run can be killed and restarted without double-writing, and audited the pipeline's own monitoring. The audit found a success signal that reported green on zero output, and one malformed bill that truncated, failed to parse, reappeared as a delta and failed again for six days. The fixes: completion requires a non-zero output count, and a length guard plus a retry ceiling parks a record that keeps failing. Then QA's accessibility review: all 26 findings resolved across five deployments, and 21 defects resubmitted, each with a written root cause and fix.

cards.answer: I design the handoff into the architecture, so the receiving team inherits contracts instead of one person's memory. On the archival build, each of the eight stages has a named owner, a gate condition that defines done, and a stated dependency, and the manifest schema assigns every column to exactly one stage, so the Library's engineer can take over one stage at a time without touching the others. The repository is the single source of truth: design docs, owner-assigned worksheets, a README for each proof of concept stating what's reusable and what's known to be broken, and 23 seed issues across five milestones, each with dependencies and "done when" criteria. Board maintenance runs through GitHub Actions. For the retirement report the runbook is executable: a preflight script checks the database client, credentials, imports and directories before the first scheduled run.

cards.answer: I make checks cheap enough to run every time. On the retirement rebuild I froze the report as a machine-checkable output contract (4 files, 21 sheets, 436 columns) validated against two earlier production outputs on every run, plus a preflight script that verifies the Oracle client, credentials, imports and distribution list before the first scheduled run, not at 6 AM on a quarter boundary. That contract caught its own bug: a floating-point equality check that passed at 224 rows and failed at 225, now a tolerance with a printed drift. On the archival build, a 50-row synthetic fixture and a deliberately broken variant let the whole suite run with no drive, no Box access and no credentials. Database writes print rollback SQL and verify row counts. Accessibility fixes were checked in a headless browser running the production Streamlit version.

cards.answer: I check coverage against what should exist, beyond what happened to load. The legislative training corpus looked complete until I measured passed-bill coverage: 1.2%. The cause was a status filter dropping every resolved bill; rebuilding took the corpus from 46,815 to 117,722 bills and coverage to 100%. The same audit found resolutions pooled with bills, which inflated the success rate to 30.4% from a true 13.2%. On the archival build, the Box accessions turned out to be extracts copied from drives: no system files, possibly flattened folders, original filesystem metadata gone. They're fine to build and test against but can't validate the reduction rate, so every derived number is marked provisional until a full drive is processed. In the HR warehouse I found two incompatible service-year definitions, which can mix age as of today with service as of another date, and logged it for the warehouse team.

cards.answer: Version one answers the customer's core question end to end on real data, once. The legislative proof of concept in February 2026 was a one-time run across ten years of Illinois legislation with a small Llama 3.2 3B pipeline: feature extraction, standardization, dashboards and vector search. IGPA approved it, and only then did I rebuild ingestion, chunking, extraction and embedding for production on the L4 server. For bill prediction I prototyped the monitoring view as a standalone HTML page over 6,556 active bills before committing it to Streamlit; that prototype defined the interaction model that shipped. On the archival build I deferred a local appraisal agent to version 2 with one constraint: no version 1 decision may preclude it. It came with a finding that matters for v1 too: agent loops belong at folder level rather than per file, where many model calls per file would turn hours into weeks.

cards.answer: Order the recovery by how fast the evidence decays. When the KNIME environment was decommissioned, the retirement workflow, its SQL, model and documentation went with it. I did SQL forensics first, from server job-history snapshots and DEBUG logs that record executed SQL verbatim, because query text disappears soonest. I reconstructed the specification from surviving output workbooks, a 2022 stakeholder presentation and recovered handoff notes, then froze it as a machine-checkable contract. I skipped a like-for-like KNIME rebuild: with the workflow gone, the usual reason to stay in KNIME didn't apply, and rebuilding twice would have been waste. Recovery surfaced knowledge that lived nowhere in code, like an employee class code that means retiree and must be excluded. The Python rebuild reproduced the legacy bracket figures 120 of 120 across two runs, and the overdue report went out the same day.

cards.answer: QA's audit returned 26 findings. I resolved all of them across five deployments between September 15 and October 2, 2026, and verified each fix in a headless browser running the production Streamlit version rather than in local code, plus a custom 14-check console tool. That reached zero automated violations on all seven pages with axe-core, the engine behind QA's Accessibility Insights, confirmed on the live site. A page-by-page walkthrough found about two dozen more issues: five contrast failures, a keyboard trap and a word cloud that rendered blank. One chart crashed and was rebuilt as accessible SVG with a data table. Reviewing QA's own screenshots and screen-reader videos surfaced three defects no earlier pass caught, and I resubmitted 21 with root cause and fix. I wrote an Accessibility Guide into the codebase for future contributors.

cards.answer: I keep the customer-specific part thin, on top of contracts that carry over. Every scheduled pipeline on our server writes Parquet logs to one schema, with PIPELINE_START and PIPELINE_END sentinel rows sharing a run ID, so a new pipeline is monitorable from day one by adding one path to the monitor's config. Onboarding the quarterly retirement pipeline needed only a per-pipeline silence threshold of 2,400 hours, since the default 48-hour rule would alert for 89 days after every run. The legislative pipeline takes a multi-state config.json, so it is ready for California expansion, and its inference router switches serving stacks by flag. When the SPA research funding platform was re-scoped, reusing the existing ingestion pipeline, NLP outputs and on-prem inference pattern took it from a 480-hour proposal to a 237-hour work request without removing functionality.

cards.answer: For payroll the interface is a Box folder. The old CPA and PUA processing was manual and semi-manual in Excel. I rebuilt it as a Python transformation framework that applies the business-rule mappings, deduplication and derived fields, with Box for both source and destination: staff upload files and processing follows. File type is detected from the naming convention, so nobody configures which kind of file it is, which removes a whole class of operator error. A GitHub Actions workflow gives one-click execution with no local environment to set up, and every output is timestamped and versioned so any run can be traced and repeated. Processing went from hours to minutes. The same idea runs through my other work: the legislative backfill went from a hand-staged chain to one command per General Assembly session.

links.label: Archival images and the production build

cards.answer: The Library engineer's university-standard laptop has integrated graphics and no discrete GPU, which rules out local high-throughput serving and makes local multimodal inference impractical. So Colab's T4 is her primary compute, and her local plan is CPU-first: a small text model, a small vision model and local embeddings, called through the Ollama HTTP API. Not the CLI, because the CLI reloads model weights on every call, which is exactly what produced 34.8 seconds per row in the email proof of concept. Real archival content can't go to Google infrastructure, so I built her a validation kit with a synthetic corpus, scoring code, notebook, rubric and brief. The working rules are explicit: credentials in a secrets manager, never a notebook cell; outputs cleared before commit; jobs checkpointed to resume; and no accession content in any public repository.

cards.title: Enforcing a customer's data boundary in code
questions: how do you keep customer data inside their boundary

links.label: Archival images and the production build

cards.answer: I enforce the boundary mechanically, because a promise doesn't survive a busy week. On the archival build, hosted AI services are excluded: models, embeddings, extracted text, the vector index and the originals stay inside the institutional network, with written confirmation sought from Data Privacy and Governance. The public demonstration build is produced by a sanitizer that refuses to write if any identifying content survives. Before publishing the repository I caught a notebook with 377 MB of embedded outputs that would have put email content in public. For document intelligence, the rule is that AI coding assistants write and run code but see aggregate metrics only; local models do all reading, and a privacy gate script denies institutional identifiers before anything reaches GitHub. On the retirement pipeline, output pairs names with salary, so credentials live outside the repository and every extract is gitignored.

secondary key rotation

cards.answer: Secrets live in platform configuration or files outside the repository, never in code or notebooks. The legislative platform's secret surface spans Cosmos keys, Azure OpenAI keys, Communication Services connection strings and deployment credentials, all held in App Service and Function App configuration, with a rotation practice that uses secondary keys so a rotation causes no downtime. The research proposals pipeline loads database credentials through a YAML config loader. The retirement pipeline keeps them in a restricted environment file outside the repository, and its preflight verifies they load before the first scheduled run. Before sharing the prediction training code with outside collaborators, I removed an embedded API key, storage credentials and local file paths. For the Library's engineer the rule is written down: credentials go in a secrets manager, never a notebook cell.

cards.title: Designing for graceful degradation
questions: what if the model is down
how do you design for graceful degradation
what happens when the llm is offline
how do you keep a pipeline stage from taking down the rest
fallbacks when an api key is missing
decoupling optional ai features
how did procurement handle the llm being down
how does she keep systems useful when a component fails
failure isolation between pipeline stages
the system never returns nothing
partial availability design
cards.answer: Every AI component should be optional to the core path. In procurement, Tier 1 exact matching on manufacturer and part number always runs, under 2 ms, even when the LLM is offline; semantic candidates still display for manual review, so the system never returns nothing. In the legislative app, LLM briefings run on open-weights Llama through Groq and degrade cleanly when no API key is configured. The automated bill investigator is deliberately decoupled from the nightly scoring core, so a failure in deep-dive generation can't take down routine scoring, and its reader layer deploys independently. The monitoring side follows the same rule: an unreadable log file becomes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record and an alert, instead of disappearing.

cards.answer: Size from the workload's real constraint, usually memory at startup for these apps, and give the decision-maker the cost trade-off in writing. The legislative app loads ML artifacts and data on start, so I evaluated Basic against Premium v3 for that memory-bound profile, wrote the cost and scaling analysis, and recommended the upgrade; it resolved the crash and cold-start cluster. Earlier I had made code changes for the Basic tier's constraints: pyarrow column pruning for selective parquet reads, cached loading, and sampling for cold starts. For procurement I designed the production deployment path: App Service B3 because the FAISS index needs 8 GB of RAM at minimum, Blob Storage for the index and parquet files, and Azure OpenAI gpt-4o-mini replacing the local model, estimated at about $77 a month.

cards.title: Debugging in an environment you don't control
questions: how do you debug in an environment you don't control
how do you troubleshoot customer infrastructure
how do you separate environment problems from code bugs
debugging without admin access
how do you diagnose a network block precisely
integration friction versus real defects
how does she debug problems on someone else's server
how do you prove which layer is failing
what's your method for environment issues
debugging a managed cloud service
cards.answer: I narrow the problem to a layer I can prove, then hand the owner of that layer evidence rather than a symptom. Three patterns recur. Network: on two occasions a destination failed at the TLS handshake while neighbors worked (Hugging Face but not GitHub or PyPI; Cosmos DB but not Blob), and testing each endpoint separately turned a vague "it can't connect" into a specific constraint I could design around or raise as an exception. Dependencies: the vLLM stand-up failed three ways at once, all version drift and VRAM contention rather than engine bugs, so I fixed them in order instead of patching code. Platform behavior: a deploy that looked like a code regression was stale workers serving old code. And the host itself: an 11-night silent failure traced to a kernel update disabling the GPU driver, documented for the system administrators.
